requirements: The core contributions of 'Fine-tuning Reinforcement Learning Models is Secretly a Forgetting Mitigation Problem' have been reproduced, demonstrating that vanilla fine-tuning of pre-trained RL models forgets pre-trained capabilities (state coverage gap and imperfect cloning gap) and that knowledge retention techniques (EWC, BC, KS, EM) mitigate this across NetHack, Montezuma's Revenge, and RoboticSequence, including a 2x state-of-the-art improvement on NetHack Human Monk.

sub_tasks.requirements: The four knowledge retention methods used for fine-tuning are correctly implemented: Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC), behavioral cloning (BC), kickstarting (KS), and episodic memory (EM), each applied only to the actor and not the critic.

Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC) is implemented as a regularization loss added to the actor's training objective that penalizes deviation of actor parameters from their pre-trained values, weighted by the diagonal Fisher information matrix estimated from the pre-trained policy, applied only to the actor and not the critic.

Behavioral cloning (BC) is implemented as a loss term added to the actor's objective that minimizes the KL divergence (or equivalent cross-entropy) between the fine-tuned actor's output distribution and the frozen pre-trained policy's output distribution on states sampled from a replay/demonstration buffer of pre-training data, applied only to the actor and not the critic.

Kickstarting (KS) is implemented as a loss term added to the actor's objective that minimizes the KL divergence between the fine-tuned actor's output distribution and the frozen pre-trained policy's output distribution evaluated on states visited online by the current fine-tuning policy (rather than on a fixed pre-training dataset), applied only to the actor and not the critic.

Episodic memory (EM) is implemented by maintaining a replay buffer populated with transitions/experience from the pre-trained policy (or pre-training environment) and mixing samples from this buffer with online fine-tuning samples during actor updates, applicable only in off-policy algorithms with a replay buffer (used with SAC in RoboticSequence), applied only to the actor and not the critic.

For all four knowledge retention methods (EWC, BC, KS, EM), the regularization/auxiliary loss or replay mechanism is applied exclusively to the actor network's parameters and updates, and the critic network is trained purely on the fine-tuning objective without any retention regularization.

Kickstarting (KS) is correctly omitted/not reported for Montezuma's Revenge and RoboticSequence experiments, consistent with the paper's statement that KS fails in the state coverage gap setting because it tries to match the pre-trained model's outputs on CLOSE states not present during pre-training.

Episodic memory (EM) is correctly implemented and applied only for RoboticSequence (using SAC's off-policy replay buffer), and is not applied for NetHack (APPO) or Montezuma's Revenge (PPO), since EM cannot be trivially applied to on-policy algorithms.

The NetHack Human Monk fine-tuning environment is set up with the Tuyls et al. (2023) pre-trained policy, APPO fine-tuning, NLD-AA dataset for retention, and the correct architecture and hyperparameters, with CLOSE/FAR defined as first level vs subsequent levels.

The NetHack Learning Environment (NLE) is used with the 'score' task, where the environmental reward is based on the increase in in-game score between time steps, and the action space consists of 120 discrete actions.

CLOSE states are defined as the set of states corresponding to the first dungeon level (since the pre-trained policy rarely leaves it, as shown in Figure 4), and FAR states are defined as states from subsequent levels.
The Human Monk character is used for all NetHack experiments, chosen because it does not require inventory management and was extensively evaluated in prior work.

The pre-trained policy π* is obtained from Tuyls et al. (2023), a model scaled up to 33M parameters (from the original 6M parameter 'Chaotic Dwarven GPT-5' baseline), trained via behavioral cloning on 115B environment transitions from the AutoAscend bot, achieving a score of over 5K points.
The NetHack model architecture is implemented following Tuyls et al. (2023) and Petrenko et al. (2020), consisting of a joint backbone shared by actor and critic with an LSTM core.

The NetHack model architecture uses a single joint backbone (encoders + LSTM core) that is shared between the actor and the critic, rather than separate networks for each, following Tuyls et al. (2023) and Petrenko et al. (2020).

An LSTM network serves as the recurrent core of the architecture, receiving the merged encoder representations as input and maintaining recurrent state across the unroll_length of 32 timesteps, following the Sample Factory (Petrenko et al., 2020) based architecture used by Tuyls et al. (2023).

The overall architecture is based on the 'Chaotic Dwarven GPT-5' solution built on Sample Factory (Petrenko et al., 2020), as scaled up and modified by Tuyls et al. (2023) from 6M to 33M parameters, and this scaled architecture (not a smaller or different variant) is the one implemented for fine-tuning.

The main dungeon screen observation is processed by embedding each character and color via an embedding lookup table into a grid, which is then processed by a ResNet encoder, following Tuyls et al. (2023).
The blstats (player status information such as health and hunger) and message (textual notifications/warnings) inputs are each processed using a separate two-layer MLP.
The encoded representations from the dungeon screen, blstats, and message encoders are merged/concatenated before being passed into an LSTM network.
The LSTM output is fed into two separate heads: a policy head and a baseline (value) head, with a shared backbone for both actor and critic.

The NLD-AA subset of the NetHack Learning Dataset (Hambro et al., 2022c) is used for knowledge retention methods, using approximately 8000 games of Human Monk collected from the AutoAscend bot, containing state-action-score transitions.
Prior to full fine-tuning, the baseline (value) head is pre-trained for 500M environment steps while freezing the rest of the model, to improve stability at the start of fine-tuning.

Fine-tuning is performed using Asynchronous Proximal Policy Optimization (APPO) (Petrenko et al., 2020), a highly parallelizable architecture capable of running over 500 million environment steps in under 24 hours on an A100 GPU.
For Fine-tuning + KS, the auxiliary KL loss is computed on data generated by the online policy, scaled by a factor of 0.5 with exponential decay of 0.99998 applied every training step.
For Fine-tuning + BC, the auxiliary KL loss is computed using trajectories generated by the AutoAscend expert algorithm (no decay applied), scaled by a factor of 2.0.
For Fine-tuning + EWC, the regularization coefficient is set to 2·10^6.
During fine-tuning with knowledge retention methods, the encoders are frozen for training stability, and entropy regularization is turned off, following the approach of Baker et al. (2022).

Per-level evaluation is implemented using the AutoAscend expert to generate 200 game saves per level (level 4 and Sokoban level), loading the agent from where the expert finished and reporting the score achieved on top of the expert's score, with models evaluated every 25 million environment steps.

The Montezuma's Revenge fine-tuning environment is set up using PPO with Random Network Distillation, a policy pre-trained from Room 7 onward, and BC data from a pre-trained agent, with CLOSE/FAR defined as pre-Room-7 vs Room-7-and-later rooms.

Montezuma's Revenge from the Atari Learning Environment (ALE) is used as the environment, characterized by extremely sparse rewards where the player controls Panama Joe navigating a labyrinthine Aztec temple.

Rooms are enumerated according to the progression shown in Figure 12 (Appendix B.2), starting from Room 1 where the player begins gameplay, defining a consistent room numbering scheme used throughout the experiments.

Successful completion of a room is defined as achieving at least one of: earning a coin as a reward, acquiring a new item, or exiting the room through a different passage than the one used to enter, used for the Room 7 success rate evaluation in Figure 6.
The room completion criterion implementation checks whether the agent earned a coin as a reward within the room episode, counting this as one valid condition for successful room completion.

The room completion criterion implementation checks whether the agent acquired a new item (e.g., key, sword, torch) within the room episode, counting this as one valid condition for successful room completion.

The room completion criterion implementation checks whether the agent exited the room through a different passage than the one used to enter it, counting this as one valid condition for successful room completion.

The room completion criterion is implemented as a logical OR (at least one condition suffices) across the three conditions (coin reward, new item, different exit passage), not requiring all three simultaneously, matching the 'at least one of' phrasing used for the Room 7 success rate evaluation in Figure 6.

CLOSE states are defined as rooms preceding Room 7 (the rooms encountered before pre-training's starting point), and FAR states are defined as Room 7 and all subsequent rooms, since the policy was pre-trained starting from Room 7 onward.

A policy π* is pre-trained on a restricted part of the environment that includes only rooms from Room 7 onward, such that during fine-tuning the agent must solve the whole game starting from Room 1, while π* only knows how to act from Room 7 onward.

The fine-tuning algorithm is PPO combined with Random Network Distillation (RND) for exploration, following Burda et al. (2018), used because Montezuma's Revenge is a sparse-reward environment where exploration is essential.

The base fine-tuning reinforcement learning algorithm used for Montezuma's Revenge is Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), providing the policy gradient updates using the combined extrinsic and intrinsic rewards.

Random Network Distillation (RND) is combined with PPO specifically because Montezuma's Revenge is a sparse-reward environment where exploration is essential, following Burda et al. (2018), and this combination (not PPO alone) is used as the fine-tuning algorithm for all Montezuma's Revenge experiments including vanilla fine-tuning and knowledge-retention variants.

The total reward signal used for PPO updates is a combination of the extrinsic (environment) reward and the intrinsic (RND prediction-error-based) reward, combined using separate value heads and discount factors (Gamma for extrinsic, IntGamma for intrinsic, per Table 2) as in the standard RND formulation of Burda et al. (2018).
The RND target network is a randomly initialized, fixed neural network that takes an observation as input and outputs a vector of size 512, and is never updated during training.

The RND prediction network takes the same observation as input, outputs a vector of size 512, and is trained via regression to predict the target network's fixed random output; the prediction error is used as an intrinsic reward signal to prioritize exploration of novel states where prediction error is high.

For behavioral cloning, more than 500 trajectories are collected from a pre-trained PPO+RND agent that achieved an episode cumulative reward of around 7000, used to populate the buffer S_BC / B_BC of states and expert actions for the BC auxiliary loss.

The RoboticSequence multi-stage Meta-World task (hammer, push, peg-unplug-side, push-wall) is implemented with SAC, a policy pre-trained on the last two stages, custom terminal-state and augmented-reward handling, and the correct MLP architecture per Algorithm 1.

RoboticSequence is built on top of the Meta-World benchmark (Yu et al., 2020), using four constituent tasks: hammer (hammer in a nail), push (push an object from one place to another), peg-unplug-side (remove a bolt from a wall), and push-wall (push an object around a wall).

RoboticSequence is built on top of the Meta-World benchmark (Yu et al., 2020), which provides the underlying simulated robotic manipulation environments and task definitions used to construct the four constituent stages.
The 'hammer' task is implemented as a constituent stage of RoboticSequence, in which the robot must hammer in a nail, using the corresponding Meta-World hammer environment.
The 'push' task is implemented as a constituent stage of RoboticSequence, in which the robot must push an object from one place to another, using the corresponding Meta-World push environment.
The 'peg-unplug-side' task is implemented as a constituent stage of RoboticSequence, in which the robot must remove a bolt from a wall, using the corresponding Meta-World peg-unplug-side environment.
The 'push-wall' task is implemented as a constituent stage of RoboticSequence, in which the robot must push an object around a wall, using the corresponding Meta-World push-wall environment.

The four constituent tasks (hammer, push, peg-unplug-side, push-wall) are arranged in this fixed order as the sequence of stages in RoboticSequence, consistent with the pre-trained policy being trained only on the last two stages (peg-unplug-side and push-wall) as described elsewhere in the paper.

Algorithm 1 (RoboticSequence) is implemented: given a list of N environments E_k, a policy pi, and time limit T, the agent steps through environment E_i using pi; if E_i is solved, it advances to the next environment and resets the timestep counter; the loop continues while i <= N and t <= T, and the number of solved environments (i-1) is returned.

Algorithm 1 is implemented such that at each timestep t, the agent steps through the current environment E_i (the i-th environment in the ordered list of N environments) using the policy pi, receiving an observation, reward, and success signal from that specific environment instance.

Algorithm 1 is implemented such that when environment E_i is solved (success condition met), the agent advances to the next environment E_{i+1} (increments i) and resets the per-stage timestep counter t to 0, so that the time limit T applies freshly to each new stage.

Algorithm 1's main loop continues executing while both i <= N (there remain unsolved environments in the sequence) and t <= T (the per-stage time limit has not been exceeded), and terminates as soon as either condition becomes false.

Algorithm 1 returns the number of successfully solved environments in the sequence, computed as (i-1) at the point the loop terminates, representing how far along the ordered sequence of N stages the agent progressed before failing to solve a stage within the time limit T or completing all stages.

Algorithm 1's return value is computed as (i-1), where i is the index of the environment in the sequence that the loop was on when it terminated, either because a stage was not solved within the time limit T or because all N stages were completed.

The returned value of Algorithm 1 correctly represents the number of successfully solved environments in the ordered sequence of N stages, i.e., the count of stages solved before failing to solve a stage within time limit T or completing the full sequence.
The start and goal conditions for each stage are randomly sampled (rather than fixed), following the same approach as in Wolczyk et al. (2021), to make the problem more challenging.

Unlike the original Meta-World environments that run indefinitely (with SAC bootstrapping the Q-value target as if non-terminal at the fixed 200-step cutoff), RoboticSequence terminates the episode and signals a true terminal state to SAC in exactly two cases: when the agent succeeds at the current stage, or when the time limit T=200 is reached, so that no bootstrapping occurs in the target Q-value in either case.

The original Meta-World environments run indefinitely at the fixed 200-step cutoff without signaling a true terminal state, such that a standard SAC implementation would bootstrap the Q-value target at the final step as if the episode were non-terminal (continuing); this default behavior is understood and contrasted against RoboticSequence's modified terminal-state handling.

RoboticSequence signals a true terminal state (done=True, with no bootstrapped Q-value target used for that transition) to SAC when the agent succeeds at the current stage, rather than continuing to bootstrap as the original Meta-World environments would.

RoboticSequence signals a true terminal state (done=True, with no bootstrapped Q-value target used for that transition) to SAC when the per-stage time limit T=200 is reached without success, rather than treating the timeout as a non-terminal truncation that would otherwise be bootstrapped.

In the SAC target Q-value computation, no bootstrapping term (discounted next-state value) is included for transitions where the episode terminates for either of the two reasons (stage success or time limit T=200 reached), consistent with signaling a true terminal state in both cases.
To keep the MDP fully observable given the modified terminal-state handling, the normalized timestep (current timestep divided by the maximal number of steps T=200) is appended to the state vector.

When an episode ends in success, the agent receives an augmented 'remaining' reward equal to r'_t = beta * r_t * (T - t), with beta = 1.5, to prevent the policy from avoiding task completion in order to keep collecting per-step rewards.
Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) (Haarnoja et al., 2018a) is used as the RL algorithm for all RoboticSequence/Meta-World experiments, with the entropy coefficient tuned automatically (Haarnoja et al., 2018b).

The policy and Q-value function are implemented as 4-hidden-layer MLPs with 256 neurons each and Leaky-ReLU activations, with layer normalization applied after the first layer, matching the Continual World (Wolczyk et al., 2021) architecture.

A separate output head is created for each stage in both the policy and Q-value networks, and the stage ID is used to select the correct head at each timestep, rather than concatenating the stage ID into the observation vector (found to work better in the paper).
SAC is trained with learning rate 1e-3 using the Adam optimizer and a batch size of 128, as specified in Appendix B.3.

The pre-trained policy pi_star is trained with SAC on only the last two stages of the sequence (peg-unplug-side and push-wall) until convergence, defined as reaching 100% success rate, and this policy is used as the starting point for all RoboticSequence fine-tuning experiments.
The observation space consists of the current robot configuration information as defined in Meta-World (Yu et al., 2020), concatenated with the stage ID encoded as a one-hot vector.

For EWC on RoboticSequence, the actor regularization coefficient is set to 100, the critic regularization coefficient is set to 0 (no critic regularization), and no memory buffer is used, per Table 3.
For BC on RoboticSequence, the actor regularization coefficient is set to 1, the critic regularization coefficient is set to 0, and a memory of 10,000 samples is used, per Table 3.

For EM on RoboticSequence, a memory of 10,000 state-action-reward tuples sampled from the pre-trained stages using the pre-trained policy is used, kept protected in SAC's replay buffer of total size 100,000 (so old samples constitute 10% of the buffer) throughout training on the downstream task, per Table 3.

Following Wolczyk et al. (2022), knowledge retention methods (EWC, BC, EM) are applied only to the actor and not to the critic in RoboticSequence, i.e. no distillation loss or L2 parameter distance regularization is applied to the critic-specific parameters.
All RoboticSequence experiments are run with at least 20 seeds, and results are presented with 90% confidence intervals, as stated in Appendix B.3.
